steps.body:
Optimisation is not a calculus problem. It is a **translation** problem with a calculus step in the middle.

1. Name what you are maximising. Write it as a formula.
2. Use the constraint to eliminate variables until **one** is left.
3. State the **domain** — the values that actually make physical sense.
4. *Then* differentiate.

Most marks are lost in steps 2 and 3, before any calculus happens.

explanationVariants: The two numbers sum to 20, so if one is x the other is 20 − x. The product is P = x(20 − x) — one variable, and the constraint has been used up.
The constraint is not an extra condition to remember; it is the tool that removes a variable.

widget.prompt: Two numbers add to 20. After using the constraint, which one-variable objective should you maximise?

options.label: P(x) = x(20 − x)
options.feedback: Right — the constraint has been consumed to eliminate the second number. One variable, and now calculus can start.

options.label: P(x, y) = xy
options.feedback: Two variables is one too many. Use x + y = 20 to write y = 20 − x, and the problem collapses to a single variable.

options.label: P(x, y) = x + y = 20
options.feedback: That is the CONSTRAINT, not the quantity you want to maximise. It is fixed at 20 — there is nothing to optimise about it.

options.label: P(x) = 20 − x
options.feedback: That is the second number, not the product. The product multiplies them.

widget.prompt: Why the physical domain decides the answer.

panels.title: The formula does not know
panels.body: For the open box, V = x(12 − 2x)². Substitute x = 100 and the algebra cheerfully returns a huge positive volume. But you cannot cut a 100-inch square out of a 12-inch sheet.

panels.title: The domain says so
panels.body: The cut must be positive (x > 0) and must leave a base (12 − 2x > 0, so x < 6). The physical domain is 0 < x < 6, and everything outside it is fiction.

panels.title: And it changes the answer
panels.body: Without the domain you might report a critical point that lies outside it — a perfect, meaningless answer. State the domain BEFORE differentiating, and the calculus can only ever hand you a legal candidate.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the third panel is where the marks are lost.
widget.successFeedback: The formula will happily compute nonsense. The domain is what stops you reporting it.

steps.body: The reveal said the domain decides. Build V′'s sign chart yourself and watch the chart claim a third region the box cannot enter.

predict.prompt: V = x(12 − 2x)², so V′ = 12(x − 2)(x − 6). The chart will show V′ turning positive again past x = 6. Does the box start growing again there?

options.label: Yes — positive V′ means growing volume
No — past 6 the base is gone; that region is fiction
No — the chart must be wrong about the sign

predict.reveal: The algebra is right AND the region is fiction — both at once. At x = 6 the base 12 − 2x is zero: no box exists there or beyond. The chart reports the formula faithfully; the DOMAIN 0 < x < 6 says which columns describe a real box. That is why you state it before differentiating.

widget.prompt: Assign V′ its sign on each interval. Roots at x = 2 and x = 6, leading coefficient positive.
widget.successFeedback: + − + : the volume rises to x = 2, falls after — so x = 2 is the maximum, V(2) = 2·8² = 128. And the final + column? The formula is happy there, but 12 − 2x < 0 means no base: the domain 0 < x < 6 has already thrown that region out. The chart shows exactly why the domain is part of the answer.
widget.crossFeedback: Check the signs by testing a point in each interval: V′(1) = 12(−1)(−5) > 0, V′(4) = 12(2)(−2) < 0, V′(7) = 12(5)(1) > 0. Both roots are single, so the sign flips at each crossing.
widget.bounceFeedback: Both roots here have multiplicity 1 — odd — so the sign CROSSES at each. A bounce (sign kept) only happens at an even-multiplicity root, and there are none in V′.

explanationVariants: The cut x must be positive, and the remaining base 12 − 2x must also be positive — so x < 6. The domain is 0 < x < 6.
At x = 6 the base has shrunk to nothing and the box has no volume at all. It is the degenerate end.

widget.prompt: A 12-inch square sheet, with squares of side x cut from the corners and the sides folded up. What is the largest x can be?

commonErrors.feedback: The sheet is only 12 inches wide, and you cut x from BOTH sides — so the base is 12 − 2x, which must be positive: x < 6.
Nothing forces x below 3. The base 12 − 2x is still positive at x = 5, though the box is getting very shallow.
That is the lower limit, not the upper one.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The base is 12 − 2x, which must be positive: x < 6.

steps.body:
Once you have one variable and a domain, the rest is chapter 1:

Differentiate. Set to zero. Find the critical points **inside the domain**. Compare their values with the values at the ends.

That is the **closed-interval method**, and it is the whole of the calculus in an optimisation problem.

explanationVariants: Differentiating a two-variable formula gets you nowhere: you must eliminate first. And a critical point outside the domain is not a candidate at all.
The calculus is easy. Getting the right thing to differentiate is the work.

widget.prompt: Put an optimisation problem in the right order.

items.label: Write a formula for the quantity to be optimised
Differentiate, and compare critical points with the endpoints
Use the constraint to reduce it to ONE variable

misorderFeedback.feedback: You cannot differentiate a formula with two variables in it. Eliminate one first.
You cannot state the domain of a formula you have not written yet.

widget.missFeedback: Formula, then constraint, then domain, then calculus.
widget.successFeedback: Formula, constraint, domain, calculus. Three translation steps and one differentiation.

steps.body: Set it up and solve it.
hints: P = x(20 − x) = 20x − x². The domain is 0 ≤ x ≤ 20.
P′ = 20 − 2x = 0 gives x = 10, the only critical point.
explanationVariants: P(10) = 10 × 10 = 100, which beats both endpoints (0 and 0). The maximum product is 100.
The two numbers are EQUAL at the optimum — which is not a coincidence, and it happens in a surprising number of these problems.

widget.prompt: Two numbers add to 20. What is their largest possible product?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the SUM, which is fixed and cannot be optimised. The product is x(20 − x), maximised at 100.
That is the value of x at the optimum. Its PRODUCT with 20 − x = 10 is 100.
That is 9 × 11 — close, but the true maximum is at 10 × 10 = 100. Equal numbers win.

takeaways: Write the quantity, use the constraint to reach ONE variable, state the physical domain, then differentiate.
The formula will happily return nonsense outside the domain — the domain is what stops you reporting it.
Once you are down to one variable on a closed interval, it is the closed-interval method from chapter 1.
steps.teaser: Next: the classic box, and the sign chart that settles it.

concept.body: Two variables cannot be differentiated. The constraint exists to KILL one of them — solve it for the variable you do not want, substitute, and only then reach for calculus.

explanationVariants: x + y = 12 gives y = 12 − x, so the product is x(12 − x).
One substitution, one variable, and the problem is ready for calculus.

widget.prompt: Two numbers add to 12. Write their product with ONE variable.

options.label: P = x(12 − x)
options.feedback: Right — the constraint has been used to eliminate y.

options.label: P = xy
options.feedback: Still two variables. Use x + y = 12 to replace y with 12 − x.
